## Analysis Results

# Palisades Fire Damage Review: Via de la Paz, Bowdoin St and Swarthmore Ave area

**About this report:** The metadata gives no capture dates, resolution or coordinates. I've written this as of shortly after January 7, 2025, and set aside any source dated January 7, 2025 or later, or with no date. I estimated coordinates from the street names in the image (Via de la Paz, Bowdoin St, Swarthmore Ave, Haverford Ave, La Cruz Dr, Patterson Pl). Without a scale I can't measure distances in meters, so spacing is described by comparison with other features in the image.

---

## Step 1: What the images show, area by area

**Burned (red), 57 labeled.** The after image shows debris and ash on nearly every lot in all four blocks: Haverford Ave, both sides of Via de la Paz, and Swarthmore Ave. This includes:
- the flat-roofed row of buildings (#52) and the long brown-roofed building (#18) west of Via de la Paz;
- the pink-roofed building (#30);
- the long building at the top of the image (#36);
- the red-tile complex east of Swarthmore (#59).

Several burned buildings had reddish, tile-colored roofs in the before image (#30, #44, #58, #59).

**Survived (green), 8 labeled:**
- **#8:** Large flat white-roofed building at Swarthmore and La Cruz. It looks commercial, not a home. It's surrounded by pavement and parking, and it's intact in the after image.
- **#37:** Home just south of the large parking lot near Bowdoin and Via de la Paz. It's intact in the after image, but its roof looks yellow there and beige before. I can't tell why from the images.
- **#60:** Intact gray roof. Its neighbors to the north (#34) and south (#31) both burned. A green lawn is still visible to its east.
- **#13:** Small gray-roofed home in the Haverford block. It's intact, and green trees remain to its north.
- **#5 and #28:** Boxy, flat-roofed, newer-looking homes on the west side of Swarthmore. Both are intact, while #47 to the south and the buildings to the north burned.
- **#27 and #24:** Pitched red-tile roofs near Patterson Pl, visible in both images. Both are intact; #38 to the south burned. A cleared lot sits to the west of #27 in the before image.

**Possible labeling problems (noted, not relabeled):**
- **#56**, the L-shaped red-tile building east of Via de la Paz, is labeled burned. But its red roof looks intact in the after image. Only the separate long building to its north (#36) looks destroyed.
- Some unlabeled buildings also look intact in the after image: the long dark-roofed building just north of #37, and two structures near #13.
- #8 is labeled as a home but looks commercial.

**Trees:** Many street and yard trees still look green in the after image even where homes burned, for example along Via de la Paz near Bowdoin.

## Step 2: Tool results

- **Wind (`get_wind_data`, Santa Monica Airport station, 7.7 km away), January 7, 2025:**
  - Calm overnight.
  - From about 7 a.m., wind blew from the north to north-northeast (0–40°).
  - Sustained winds reached 13–25 mph, with gusts of 20–55 mph. The peak was 25 mph with 55 mph gusts at 9:51 p.m.
  - January 8 returned no data.
  - The station is several kilometers away, so local winds may have been different. The images don't show which way the fire actually moved.
- **Terrain (`get_terrain`), three points:** elevation 93–98 m, slope 1.3–2.5°. The land is essentially flat, so slope does not explain the differences here. (This depends on my estimated coordinates being right.)
- **Reference sources used (`get_reference_fire_findings`):**
  - **Camp Fire, 2018:** Knapp et al., *Fire Ecology*, USDA Forest Service Treesearch (research.fs.usda.gov/treesearch/65039), published 2021-09-20.
    - The strongest predictors of survival were distance to the nearest destroyed structure and the number destroyed within 100 m.
    - Homes more than 18 m from a destroyed structure survived at a much higher rate.
    - Homes built before 1997 had 11.5% survival, versus 38.5% for those built in 1997 or later.
    - Most damage to homes that survived came from the heat of nearby burning buildings, or from flames when things right next to the home caught fire.
  - **Camp Fire, 2018:** Research Square preprint of the same study (researchsquare.com/article/rs-580864/v1), published 2021-06-17. Older homes sat in denser areas and had more homes burn nearby.
  - **Tubbs Fire, 2017:** Perkins&Will Research Journal 14.01 (issuu.com), published 2022-03-31. In Coffey Park, "the fuel source shifted from trees and vegetation to buildings."
  - **Lahaina, 2023:** No usable source. Every result was undated or published after the cutoff.
- **Search results set aside:**
  - Published after the cutoff:
    - earth.com (2025-08-31)
    - squarespace blog (2026-09-02)
    - Substack (2026-11-11)
    - SGH (2025-02-20)
    - UCANR "Can homes be designed…" (2025-03-31)
    - UCANR IGIS (2025-07-10)
    - Informed Infrastructure (2025-05-27)
    - academia.edu listing (2025-05-12)
    - FEMA Maui report (2025-05-25)
    - PMC Maui article (2026-03-11)
    - frames.gov catalog page (2026-07-17; it describes a 2022 paper, but the page itself is dated after the cutoff)
  - Conflicting date: the UCANR "14,000 homes" blog is listed as 2025-03-31, but its text says December 21, 2018.
  - Date unknown:
    - MPRA papers 116166 and 104232
    - IBHS Camp Fire and Lahaina reports
    - CAL FIRE Tubbs investigation (also about the fire's cause)
    - UMD thesis
    - Maui after-action report, Maui WES health study and FEMA SR-1
    - USFS PSW PDF (same study as the dated Treesearch page, which I cite instead)
  - Off-topic: CBC (2017-12-17), which is about homes next to wildland brush, not dense neighborhoods.

---

## 1. Key takeaways
- **Nearly the whole neighborhood burned, block after block, on flat ground.** This suggests fire spread mostly from house to house, not up a hillside.
- **Several survivors sit next to non-burnable open space,** such as the large parking lot, paved areas around #8, and a cleared lot near #27. This suggests gaps in fuel helped. Some survivors (#60, #5, #28) are not explained by anything visible.
- **The images can't show roofing material ratings, vents, siding, windows or firefighting.** The most important building details for rebuilding are unknown from this data.

## 2. Why the red-outlined homes burned

I found only **two well-supported reasons**. A third would only be a guess:
- **Slope:** the land is flat (`get_terrain`), so slope is ruled out.
- **Vegetation:** I'm not ranking it. The before image shows hedges and trees between lots, but the after image shows many trees still green next to destroyed homes. That doesn't point to vegetation as the main way fire spread.
- **Home age and materials:** these can't be seen in satellite images.

**Reason 1: Homes were close together, so fire spread from one house to the next.**
- **What the images show:** In the before image, homes on all four blocks sit on narrow lots. The gaps between them look much narrower than the streets. In the after image, whole rows are destroyed with no breaks (for example #12, #15, #25 and #65 along Via de la Paz, and #2, #4, #17 and #53 east of it).
- **What this suggests:** Once one home caught fire, its heat and flames could reach the next one.
- **Reference fires:** This matches the Camp Fire (Knapp et al., 2021), where distance to the nearest destroyed building was a top predictor. It also matches the Tubbs Fire account (Perkins&Will, 2022), where buildings themselves became the main fuel.

**Reason 2: Strong, dry north winds likely spread fire across the whole area.**
- **What the data and images show:** `get_wind_data` recorded north to north-northeast winds with gusts up to 55 mph on January 7. The images show destruction everywhere, including inner blocks and buildings with tile-colored roofs (#30, #59), while many trees stayed green.
- **What this suggests:** Wind-carried embers and burning homes, rather than a fire front moving through trees, likely ignited homes across the area.
- **Limits:** Wind and embers can't be seen in a photo. I found no usable ember study dated before the cutoff.

## 3. Why the green-outlined homes survived

I found **one well-supported reason and one weak one**. I couldn't support a third. Firefighter or homeowner action, vents, windows and siding can't be seen, and #60 (which survived between two burned homes) stays unexplained.

**Reason 1: Next to open space that doesn't burn.**
- **What the images show:**
  - #37 and the unlabeled building north of it sit just south of the large paved parking lot. The burned buildings #52 and #18 are on its north side.
  - #8 is surrounded by pavement and parking.
  - #27 borders a cleared lot to its west.
  - #13 sits in the same block as the parking lot.
  - The large red-tile building (#56), which looks intact but is labeled burned, stands in open paved and landscaped grounds.
- **What this suggests:** These gaps likely kept burning neighbors farther away. With the north wind, homes just south of the parking lot may have been shielded. That last point is inferred, because the images don't show which way the fire moved.
- **Reference fire:** Camp Fire homes more than 18 m from a destroyed building survived much more often (Knapp et al., 2021).

**Reason 2 (weak): Building type and roof form.**
- **What the images show:** #5 and #28 have boxy, flat roofs and look newer than their neighbors. #27 and #24 have visible red-tile roofs. #8 looks like a commercial building.
- **What this suggests:** These buildings may have been built differently. But several burned buildings also had tile-colored roofs (#30, #44, #59), and age and materials can't be confirmed from above.
- **Reference fire:** Camp Fire homes built in 1997 or later survived far more often (Knapp et al., 2021).

## 4. Summary

Almost every building in this flat, densely built neighborhood was destroyed. The after image shows unbroken rows of debris, while many trees are still green. Together with the slope readings and recorded gusts up to 55 mph, this suggests a wind-driven fire that spread from building to building.

The few survivors are mostly next to fuel-free areas: a parking lot, paved commercial grounds and a cleared lot. That pattern matches Camp Fire research showing that distance from burning buildings matters most.

Some survivals, especially #60 between two destroyed homes, can't be explained from these images. Details like vents, siding, windows, roofing ratings and firefighting may have decided individual outcomes, and none of them can be seen here.

## 5. Confidence

| Reason | Score | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Burned 1: Close spacing / house-to-house spread | **8** | Visible in the images; matches Camp Fire (2021) and Tubbs Fire (2022) sources |
| Burned 2: Wind-driven embers | **5** | Wind comes from a tool, not the images; the visible pattern is only indirect evidence; no usable ember source |
| Survived 1: Next to non-burnable open space | **6** | Visible for #37, #8, #27 and #13 and supported by Camp Fire research, but doesn't explain #60, #5 or #28 |
| Survived 2: Building type / roof form | **3** | Inferred from roof shape and color; contradicted by burned tile-colored roofs; materials not visible |

## 6. Rebuilding

Lots here are narrow, so homes can't be spread much farther apart. Rebuilding should instead stop each home from becoming fuel for the next one. The Camp Fire research found that homes that survived were mostly damaged by heat from nearby burning buildings or by things right next to them catching fire. That points to:
- fire-resistant walls and windows on the sides that face neighbors;
- non-burnable materials in the strip right around each home;
- non-burnable fences and side-yard features where neighbors' properties connect.

Homes built in 1997 or later survived far more often in Paradise (Camp Fire, Knapp et al., 2021), so building to current wildfire codes matters. Keeping and planning open, non-burnable spaces such as paved areas, cleared yards and lawns between groups of homes could help, like the parking lot that seems to have shielded nearby buildings. Because one home's ignition puts its neighbors at risk, this works best when the whole block does it together. A qualified professional should check vents, roofing and siding choices, since this report couldn't see them.

## 7. Likelihood of a similar outcome

If most homes followed these recommendations, risk would likely be **lower, but not eliminated.** These changes target the house-to-house spread that seems to have driven the losses here.

Three things would stay the same: the homes would still be close together, wind like that recorded on January 7 (gusts up to 55 mph) could happen again, and embers can still reach homes. If only a few homes upgraded, their risk would stay closer to **similar**, because burning neighbors would still be close by. The images and sources here don't support putting a number on this.
